h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: L2 shrinkage compounds multiplicatively across three weight matrices, so raising alpha drives deep nets toward output collapse much faster than shallow ones.
The penalty gradient alpha*W/batch_size is not diluted at small batches while Adam normalizes the data gradient, so an alpha increase is far more over-regularizing at batch 4-10.
In standard parameterization wider layers sum more coordinated updates per pre-activation, so widening at lr 0.278-1 pushes training into divergence rather than adding useful capacity.
Large batches give few updates in 243 epochs, and wider nets fit faster per step, so width substitutes for missing optimization steps.
Large batches leave the network undertrained with few steps, so a larger learning rate compensates, whereas at small batches the extra step size mainly adds instability.
Deeper ReLU nets realize their extra capacity only in a moderate learning-rate window, being stalled at tiny rates and divergent at huge ones.
Narrow nets are capacity-limited, so L2 binds them hardest and relaxing it frees scarce capacity, while wide nets barely notice the change.
Narrow deep ReLU stacks lose information through dead units at each bottleneck layer, so adding depth to 16-40 unit layers helps less or hurts.
Deeper nets need more optimization steps to coordinate their layers within 243 epochs, so cutting steps per epoch by enlarging the batch hurts them more.
Under heavy L2, extra width lets the function be spread over many small weights, relieving over-regularization that otherwise caps a narrower net.
